title: Article 368 — Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor

content.overview: Article 368 confers on Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and sets out the procedure. An amendment Bill may be introduced in either House; it must be passed by each House by a special majority (majority of the total membership of that House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting). For amendments of certain provisions (federal features listed in the proviso — e.g. distribution of powers, representation of States in Parliament, Supreme Court/High Courts, etc.), ratification by not less than one-half of the State Legislatures is also required before Presidential assent. The President shall give assent to a duly passed amendment Bill. The basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati) limits the amending power: Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution.
content.glance: Amendment by special majority in each House; some amendments need ratification by ≥1/2 of State Legislatures. President must assent. Basic structure cannot be amended (Kesavananda).
content.study:
Article 368 procedure:
1. Bill in either House of Parliament.
2. Special majority in each House: majority of total membership + ≥2/3 of members present and voting.
3. If the amendment falls within the proviso (federal/entrenched provisions), ratification by not less than one-half of State Legislatures by resolution.
4. Presidential assent (mandatory; no withhold/return for amendment Bills under the article’s terms as interpreted).

**Basic structure:** Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that the amending power under Article 368 does not extend to damaging or destroying the basic structure of the Constitution. Subsequent cases have elaborated elements (supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism, secularism, free and fair elections, etc.).

Examination: special majority formula; proviso (State ratification); mandatory assent; basic structure limitation; contrast ordinary legislation.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body:
1. Amendment Bill in either House.
2. Each House: majority of total membership + ≥2/3 of present and voting.
3. Proviso provisions: ratification by ≥1/2 of State Legislatures.
4. Presidential assent.
5. Limitation: basic structure cannot be destroyed (Kesavananda Bharati).

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain the procedure to amend the Constitution under Article 368.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Under Article 368, a Bill to amend the Constitution may be introduced in either House of Parliament and must be passed by each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting. If the amendment seeks to make a change in provisions specified in the proviso (federal features such as the distribution of legislative powers, representation of States in Parliament, or the High Courts/Supreme Court, among others), it must also be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States before presentation to the President for assent. The President shall give assent. The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati held that Parliament’s amending power does not extend to altering the basic structure of the Constitution.
